title: 10 Most Popular Restaurants in Silom-Sathorn 2026 — Eat Me, Le Du, Prachak Roasted Duck | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: 10 most popular restaurants in Bangkok's Silom-Sathorn district, picked from real reviews — Eat Me, Michelin-starred Le Du, the century-old Prachak Roasted Duck, Somtum Der, Baan Phadthai and Khao Tom Niyom for late-night eating. With prices, signature dishes and planning tips.
keywords: Silom restaurants, Sathorn restaurants, best restaurants Silom, Eat Me Bangkok, Le Du, Prachak Roasted Duck, Somtum Der, Baan Phadthai, Khao Tom Niyom Silom, Convent Road food, Sala Daeng food, Michelin Silom
ogTitle: 10 Most Popular Restaurants in Silom-Sathorn 2026 (picked from real reviews)
ogDesc: Michelin fine dining, a century-old roasted duck, bold Isan som tam, and late-night Chinese congee. 10 standout places in Silom-Sathorn that people who live here actually eat at — with prices and signature dishes.
eyebrow: Eat like a Silom-Sathorn local · updated 2026
intro: Silom-Sathorn is the neighbourhood where you can eat well at every price point — from the kind of Michelin fine dining that requires a reservation to a street-corner roasted duck stall you stumble into. Walking distance covers an Asia's 50 Best restaurant, a century-old duck shop, bold Isan som tam, and late-night Chinese congee. We pulled together the 10 places locals and real reviewers talk about most, so you know exactly where to go.
chips: 🌶️ Bold som tam near Sala Daeng-Convent

blocks.html:
If you had to pick one Bangkok neighbourhood that covers every mood and every budget in a single walk, Silom-Sathorn is the answer most people reach for first. At lunchtime it's a dense office district where workers spill out into every lane. Once the evening lights come on, Convent Road, Surawong, and Sala Daeng turn into a stretch of restaurants so varied it's almost overwhelming — one lane takes you past an Indian curry house, an Isan som tam stall, a thick-broth guay jub shop, crispy-skin roasted duck, and then around the corner there's a cocktail bar and a fine dining room. The draw here is that the neighbourhood never forces a choice. A hundred-baht plate by the roadside is as available as a multi-thousand-baht tasting menu, and everything is within walking distance or one BTS stop away.

What makes it even better is that many of the places here have a real story behind them. Prachak Roasted Duck has been selling the same recipe in Bang Rak for over a hundred years and is now a pilgrimage stop for duck lovers. Le Du's chef Ton once held the number-one spot on Asia's 50 Best Restaurants and has carried a Michelin star for years. Somtum Der and Baan Phadthai are both Michelin Bib Gourmand certified. Eat Me has been an institution on the Silom side of Bangkok since 1998. And Khao Tom Niyom and Somtum Convent have been feeding this neighbourhood for decades without a dip. We wanted to walk you through this area like someone who actually eats here — starting with these 10 places, you'll come away with both good food and memories that stick.

blocks.name: Eat Me Restaurant
blocks.area: Soi Piphat 2 (Convent Road), Silom, Bang Rak, Bangkok
blocks.signature: International modern seasonal menu — Australian Wagyu, raw fish, chocolate dessert — plus a cocktail bar on the ground floor
blocks.descHtml:
Opening our Silom-Sathorn list with a true institution: Eat Me is an international modern restaurant in Soi Piphat 2 (off Convent Road) that has been part of Bangkok since 1998 and still holds a place in the Michelin Guide. The room itself is part gallery, part dining room — high ceilings, exposed steel beams, low lighting, and rotating Thai art pieces on the walls. If you're after a great date-night dinner, a celebration meal, or a proper evening out for serious eaters, this is one of the first names that comes up.

Chef Tim Butler, an American who trained with Marcus Samuelsson and Daniel Boulud, runs a menu that pulls ingredients from around the world and plays them off Thai flavors in inventive ways. The dishes reviews mention most are the Australian Wagyu — Wagyu A5 tataki and a Wagyu tenderloin grilled to medium rare with a smoky barbecue sauce, the meat tender enough to earn praise from most tables. Other standouts include Manila clams with fermented pork, maitake mushrooms with Brillat-Savarin, and raw fish preparations. Desserts — including homemade chocolate creations and house ice cream — get genuinely enthusiastic reviews.

A second draw is the cocktail bar on the ground floor, which has an open-air courtyard shaded by trees. The cocktails often riff on Thai ingredients like betel leaf, and you can settle in for drinks before heading upstairs for dinner. Service is attentive without being intrusive. Prices run on the premium side — many mains are in the upper hundreds to lower thousands, and a full dinner per person typically lands around 1,200–2,500 THB. This is a place for a special occasion rather than a quick meal.

Good to know: Eat Me is dinner-only, open 17:00–01:00 daily (Sunday brunch from 11:00). The kitchen and bar take last orders around 1am. Weekends fill up fast — book ahead. English menus are available and staff handle international guests well. Parking in the lane is limited; grabbing a cab or motorbike taxi from BTS Sala Daeng or MRT Silom is more practical.

blocks.name: Le Du
blocks.signature: Seasonal Thai tasting menu using Thai ingredients — river prawns, jasmine rice, Wagyu with Thai sauce
blocks.descHtml:
Le Du is the contemporary Thai restaurant that many fine-dining regulars put first when thinking about Bangkok. Chef Ton — Thitid Tassanakajohn — trained at Eleven Madison Park in New York before coming back to bring Thai seasonal ingredients into conversation with Western technique. The name means "season" in Thai, which explains the menu: it changes several times a year to follow what's in its prime. The restaurant has held a Michelin one-star since 2019 and in 2023 was ranked number one on Asia's 50 Best Restaurants. If you're after a special meal that shows Thai cuisine in a form you haven't encountered before — a celebration dinner, a landmark evening — this is one of the most compelling options in Bangkok.

The menu is a tasting set: four or six courses. The dish almost every review mentions is the signature river prawn — a grilled river prawn finished with a tom yum sauce and prawn fat, served alongside a risotto-style khao khluk kapi (rice with shrimp paste) made with Mae Hong Son shrimp paste. Food writers who cover Thai cuisine consistently score this dish the highest of any plate in the meal and say they reorder it every visit. Another dish that draws attention in summer is the house version of khao chae — played with jasmine ice cream, pork and prawn balls, and proper khao chae accompaniments. Even the closing mango sticky rice earns compliments from non-Thai diners who say it's better than expected.

Review sentiment is largely consistent: the food is thoughtfully constructed, plated beautifully, and stays Thai at its core in flavor. Staff are well-briefed and the sommelier is genuinely worth talking to for wine pairings. Common notes include pricing that feels steep relative to portion size, and a tendency at some evening sittings to move tables along for a second seating — if that bothers you, ask for the later slot. The four-course set runs roughly 3,900 THB and the six-course around 4,500 THB, with wine pairing adding approximately 2,500 THB. Budget for it accordingly.

The restaurant is in Silom Soi 7, Bang Rak — about a four-minute walk from BTS Chong Nonsi and easy to find. Dinner is the main service: 18:00–23:00 daily, with occasional lunch sittings 12:00–14:00. Bookings are essential; it fills up almost every night despite the price. If you want to try Thai food at the Michelin level with a chef willing to take real creative risk, Le Du belongs on the short list. Allow yourself a long, unhurried evening.
mustOrder: River prawn with tom yum sauce + khao khluk kapi
Khao chae with jasmine ice cream
blocks.bestFor: Celebration dinner / special-occasion fine dining, contemporary Thai

blocks.name: Prachak Roasted Duck, Bang Rak (Prachak Pet Yang / Ped Prachak)
blocks.signature: Crispy-skin roasted duck with rich sauce, rice with duck, roasted duck noodles, char siu and crispy pork
blocks.descHtml:
Prachak Roasted Duck, Bang Rak is a Thai-Chinese roasted duck shop that has stood on Charoen Krung Road for over a hundred years — open since 1909, passing the recipe down through the family to the current generation. The shop is a classic shophouse opposite the Bang Rak Robinson, a short walk from BTS Saphan Taksin exit 3. It suits anyone who wants the legendary roasted duck in no-fuss surroundings — a first meal in the Silom-Bang Rak area, or a hearty lunch while exploring the Charoen Krung neighbourhood.

The dishes nearly every table orders are the rice with roasted duck and the roasted duck noodles. The draw is crispy duck skin, meat that falls off the bone easily, and a deeply fragrant dark sauce. Served with pickled ginger and chili-soy sauce on the side to cut the richness. Groups often order a whole duck to share, or the combined plate (known as Che Pho) that brings duck, char siu and crispy pork together on one platter. Another crowd favourite is the prawn wontons and the roasted duck noodle soup. Some reviews go so far as to say the char siu and crispy pork are as good as — or better than — the duck itself.

Most reviews agree on the same things: the duck is tender, the sauce is rich and well-spiced, the quantity is generous for the price. Rice with duck and noodles start around 79–105 THB; prawn wontons and combination plates step up a little; a whole duck is available to take away. The setting is an old, simple room with close-together tables. Lunch and dinner see a mix of neighbourhood regulars and tourists filling the place.

Good to know before you go: the duck tends to sell out — many people report that by mid-afternoon to evening the duck is gone. To get the full selection, come before noon or early afternoon. The shop is open daily roughly 08:30–20:30 but signature items may be gone before closing. Cash is easier. Parking is almost nonexistent — BTS is strongly recommended. Staff speak some English and the menu has photos and English text so ordering is manageable.
mustOrder: Che Pho platter (duck, char siu, crispy pork)
blocks.bestFor: First meal in Bang Rak-Silom, roasted duck fans
blocks.hours: 08:30–20:30 daily (duck often sells out before closing)
blocks.spice: Mild (chili-soy sauce served separately to add yourself)

blocks.name: Somtum Der, Sala Daeng branch
blocks.area: Sala Daeng Road, Silom, Bang Rak, Bangkok
blocks.signature: Crab-and-fermented-fish som tam, fried chicken, crying tiger beef, beef waterfall salad, sticky rice — proper Isan flavors
blocks.descHtml:
When it comes to a som tam shop in Bangkok where both Thais and foreigners line up in equal numbers, Somtum Der's Sala Daeng branch is one of the first names that comes up. This is the original location, opened in 2012 on a small lane off Silom Road — a short walk from BTS Sala Daeng or MRT Silom. From that small shophouse, it's now a name with branches as far as New York, Tokyo and Taipei, and it has held a Michelin Guide Bangkok listing for multiple years running. It's the place to go if you want bold Isan food in air-conditioned comfort in the middle of Silom, without compromising on the flavor.

The dish reviews mention most is the house fried chicken thigh — crispy skin, juicy meat inside, something people say they reorder every visit. Right behind it is the crying tiger beef (nuea rong hai) and the beef waterfall salad (nam tok nuea), both with tender grilled beef and good charcoal fragrance. The star of the menu is still the som tam, with over ten versions to choose from — plain Thai style, crab-and-fermented-fish som tam for a funkier finish, and Luang Prabang style for something different. If you want something unusual, the catfish floss som tam (yam pla duk foo) pairs a mound of crispy puffed catfish with a tart, spicy dressing — try it with hot sticky rice. The Isan noodle stir-fry (phat mee isan) is also a table favourite as something to share. Flavor-wise most reviews agree: punchy and full of spice, the fermented fish coming through cleanly without burying everything. Those who don't do spicy should note that this place is genuinely hot — ask to lower the chili level when ordering.

On price it's noticeably higher than roadside som tam — expect around 250–500 THB per person. The som tam starts in the hundreds, while protein dishes like crying tiger step into the upper hundreds. Against the Michelin-recognized, air-conditioned setting in the middle of Silom, most reviews consider it fair value. The interior is bright with a "metro Isan" design, and the playlist runs through a mix of mor lam and international music.

Good to know: the restaurant is small and gets crowded at weekday lunches and weekend evenings. Queues form during peak times. Open daily 11:00–23:00 with delivery available, card payment accepted and an English menu for tourists. For anyone visiting Silom-Sathorn who wants to try Michelin-certified Isan food, this is one of the clearest recommendations.
mustOrder: Crying tiger beef / beef waterfall salad
blocks.bestFor: Bold Isan food in air-con in the middle of Silom / tourists wanting a Michelin-listed experience

blocks.name: "Hai" Somtum Convent
blocks.signature: Blue crab som tam, grilled pork neck, charcoal-grilled chicken, grilled fish, grilled offal, bold Isan flavors
blocks.descHtml:
If you work around Silom-Sathorn and want bold som tam and fragrant grilled chicken without travelling far, "Hai" Somtum Convent is a name people in this neighbourhood have been talking about for nearly 30 years. The shop is in Soi Convent, opposite Park Silom — walk from BTS Sala Daeng exit 2 into the lane and you're there. It's an open-fronted shophouse with fans downstairs (Isan stall-style) and air-con upstairs for hotter days. The selling point is speed — the surrounding offices pile in for weekday lunch every day, the food comes out fast, and there's rarely a long wait.

The dishes people order most are the blue crab som tam (plenty of crab, a nicely forward sour note), the salted-egg som tam where the rich yolk plays off the dressing, grilled pork neck, charcoal-grilled chicken, pork laab, grilled catfish and grilled fish, and a tom saep pork rib soup that's sour and spicy enough to drink fast. If you like unusual things, there's sweet liver, deep-fried chicken tendons, and fermented pork to try. What reviews consistently point out is fresh ingredients — you can see bowls of raw ingredients lined up at the front — and chicken that stays juicy.

To give an honest picture: this isn't a place where every dish is perfectly consistent. Some reviews flag that the grilled pork neck can be a touch dry on a given day, and the overall flavor runs sweeter than hardcore rural Isan som tam. Prices for som tam are higher than typical roadside stalls because of the central Silom location. If you don't eat spicy, tell the staff upfront — the house standard is genuinely hot.

Per-dish prices run 40–120 THB, and a full meal averages around 150–250 THB per person — reasonable value for this central location. Open Mon–Fri roughly 10:30–21:00, with earlier closing on Saturday–Sunday (around 17:00). The weekday lunch rush is the most crowded stretch; come before noon or mid-afternoon for a calmer table. Good for office workers who want a one-plate Isan lunch, or groups sharing several Isan dishes in the middle of the city.
blocks.bestFor: Weekday office lunch / group som tam meal in the middle of Silom
blocks.spice: Very spicy Isan style (can request less spicy)
blocks.libCredit: Illustration: som tam · Vyacheslav Argenberg / Wikimedia (CC BY 4.0)

blocks.title: 🛏️ Staying in Silom-Sathorn means the whole list is walkable
blocks.text: The charm of staying in Silom-Sathorn is that almost every place on this list is within walking distance or one BTS stop. Wake up and walk to Prachak for duck rice, grab lunch at Somtum Der near Sala Daeng, then close the night at Eat Me and walk home. The neighbourhood has hotels from quiet-lane boutiques to five-star properties on Sathorn Road with direct BTS and MRT access. Pick something near a station and both eating and sightseeing become much easier.

blocks.name: The Indian Hut
blocks.signature: Butter chicken (Murgh Makhani), Dal Tadka, tandoor naan, biryani, paneer, Dahi Puri
blocks.descHtml:
When people mention Indian food in the Silom-Surawong area, The Indian Hut is one of the first names that comes up — the restaurant has been open since 1995, making it a pioneer of North Indian and Indian-Chinese food in Bangkok. The restaurant is on Surawong Road, across from Manohra Hotel and near the Silom Indian temple, a short walk from BTS Chong Nonsi or Sala Daeng. It's the right choice if you want serious, sit-down Indian food in a comfortable setting rather than a pavement stall, and it works well for groups or private dining since the restaurant has two floors and can host buffets.

The dishes reviews mention most consistently are the Butter Chicken (Murgh Makhani) — a rich, fragrant sauce that one review after another calls smooth and satisfying — the Dal Tadka, a lentil preparation seasoned hard that many people say they could just drink, and the tandoor naan, soft with charred edges (try the garlic naan or the rumali roti). The biryani — chicken and lamb — gets praise for generous meat and well-cooked rice. The vegetarian side is strong too: paneer preparations (Paneer Pasanda, Lababdar, Tikka) and Dahi Puri draw good reviews for freshness and seasoning. Grilled items like Murg Malai Kebab and Kalmi Kabab are worth adding if you want something from the tandoor.

On flavor, the Indian community's own reviewers often say this is "the best outside India" — quick service, strong spicing, and staff who are themselves Indian and attentive. One point reviewers note in the restaurant's favour: the kitchen manages spice aroma well, keeping the room from getting overwhelmingly fragrant the way some Indian restaurants do, which makes it a gentler introduction for first-timers. The setting is classic and formal — high ceilings, mirrors, fresco-style art — which some find a little old-fashioned, but the tradeoff of good food makes most people say it's worth it.

Prices sit in the mid-range: roughly 251–500 THB per person. Naan starts around 90 THB; paneer and mains run 300–400 THB; two people ordering several dishes will land around 1,000–2,000 THB including VAT and service charge. Note that VAT and service are added separately. Open daily 11:00–23:00 with parking available, card payment accepted, cocktails and alcohol available, and both vegetarian and Jain menu options. Google rating 4.3, Tripadvisor 4.3 from over 300 reviews — a solid long-standing Indian restaurant that has held its standards.
blocks.bestFor: Coming as a group / serious Indian dinner out

blocks.name: Baan Phadthai
blocks.signature: Pad Thai with an 18-ingredient sauce, river prawn pad Thai, crab pad Thai, egg-wrapped pad Thai, Thai desserts
blocks.descHtml:
If you think pad Thai is just a cheap street-food dish, Baan Phadthai in Charoen Krung 44 will change that view. The restaurant comes from the same team as Issaya Siamese Club — they took a familiar dish and built it up carefully, serving it in a restored vintage blue shophouse. The real selling point is the house pad Thai sauce, which uses 18 ingredients: Chanthaburi-style rice noodles, home-pounded dried shrimp, duck eggs, and crab roe, cooked in a crab stock instead of a prawn base, which gives a deeper, more fragrant result than you'd usually find. It's the place to take out-of-town guests for pad Thai, or simply to treat yourself to the considered version of the dish.

The dishes reviews mention most are the grilled river prawn pad Thai — large prawns, rich fat — and the crab pad Thai, heavily loaded with crab meat. Groups often order the oversized crab pad Thai, which is big enough to share across the table. The charcoal-grilled pork pad Thai is another order people return for, the pork bringing a light smoky quality. As a starter, the miang kha na works well, and mango sticky rice rounds things off. The consensus on the noodles: cooked well, holding texture without going soft, with a wok hei (charred aroma) that roadside stalls rarely achieve. The sauce balance — sour, sweet, salty — is one of the points reviews tend to highlight most.

Prices are honestly higher than a street stall: pad Thai starts around 160 THB and climbs to 250–280 THB for river prawn and crab versions. Some reviews feel the flavors have been adjusted slightly for tourist palates, and the quantity per price may not match a roadside portion — but against the quality of ingredients and the care put in, most people say it's worth it. The restaurant itself is a visual draw: a vintage Thai house painted in bright colors, photogenic inside.

Located in Charoen Krung Soi 44, Bang Rak, walkable from BTS Saphan Taksin. Michelin Bib Gourmand since 2018 — consistently one of the most talked-about pad Thai names in Bangkok. Open daily 11:00–22:00. Note: no parking at the restaurant itself; the Robinson Bang Rak car park is the closest option. Expect a wait at weekend lunches and evenings.
blocks.bestFor: Taking visitors for premium pad Thai / lunch or dinner in the Charoen Krung area

blocks.name: Guay Jub Silom, Soi Convent
blocks.area: Soi Convent, Silom, Bang Rak, Bangkok
blocks.signature: Thick-broth guay jub with plenty of toppings — crispy pork, liver and offal, boiled egg
blocks.descHtml:
Guay Jub Silom (Soi Convent) is a thick-broth guay jub shop that has been an institution in Soi Convent for over 30 years — starting as a street cart before moving into a shophouse across from Park Silom. If you work in Silom-Sathorn or just want something hot and deeply Chinese-spiced, this is the place neighbourhood regulars turn to first. The dish to order is the thick-broth guay jub with generous toppings — a full bowl with crispy pork, liver and tripe, fried tofu, and a whole boiled egg. The traditional rolled rice noodles are blanched to a soft, springy texture that traps every sip of broth.

Real reviews consistently name the broth as the star. Simmered with spices and five-spice powder until deeply fragrant, it arrives heavy with white pepper and warmth. Crispy pork is fried well — not greasy — and the offal is clean and handled well, without the off-smell that puts some people off. Another dish reviewers quietly recommend just as highly is sea bass rice porridge — clear broth, fresh fish — with some even saying the rice porridge outshines the guay jub itself. Anyone who doesn't eat offal or finds thick broth too heavy can order the clear-broth version or plain noodle soup separately.

Prices are generous: thick-broth guay jub starts around 60 THB, fully loaded bowls around 95 THB — well under a hundred baht per person. Seafood and fish rice porridge run around 125 THB per bowl. Crispy pork is also available as a side plate. The shop is a two-unit shophouse with seating on both floors, in the classic old Bangkok street-food style with close tables. The midday rush from Silom offices fills it up fast.

Location: the mouth of Soi Convent, five minutes' walk from BTS Sala Daeng or MRT Silom — easy to find right across from Park Silom. Hours: roughly 11:00–22:00. Closed Saturdays. Good to know: opening times can shift a little by day; if you're coming late or on a holiday check the page first. To avoid fighting for a table with the office crowd, sidestep the noon rush.
mustOrder: Thick-broth guay jub with full toppings (crispy pork, offal, boiled egg)
blocks.bestFor: Hot broth lunch on a workday in Silom
blocks.libCredit: Illustration: congee · Alpha from Melbourne, Australia / Wikimedia (CC BY-SA 2.0)

blocks.name: Khao Tom Niyom, Silom Plaza (Niyom / 時興飯店)
blocks.area: Silom Plaza, Silom Road, Bang Rak, Bangkok
blocks.signature: Teochew-style Chinese congee with Chinese side dishes — clams with chili paste, squid with salted egg, pork with lime, chai poh omelette
blocks.descHtml:
When people in Silom talk about the old-school khao tom kuay (Chinese congee) shop in the neighbourhood, Khao Tom Niyom (時興飯店) at Silom Plaza Ground Floor comes up first. The restaurant has been around for decades — it originally operated near Surawong Road from the founder's generation, survived a fire, then relocated to Silom Plaza with the same team and the same recipes. It's Teochew-style congee: you order thin rice congee alongside Chinese-style side dishes to eat with it. Good for an after-work dinner or a late-night meal in Silom-Sathorn, especially with a group sharing several dishes.

The dishes nearly every table orders are the clams stir-fried with chili paste — around 220 THB, large fresh clams with a deep, flavourful sauce that many say they keep reordering — followed by squid stir-fried with salted egg (fragrant and pleasantly rich), pork with lime (refreshingly tart to cut through heavier dishes), and the chai poh omelette (preserved radish omelette), a classic Thai-Chinese pairing with congee. Regular diners also order the tom moo sap kiam buay (minced pork soup with salted plum), where the kitchen gets the sweet-sour-salty balance right in a way many other places overdo the sourness. For heavier eating there's minced pork stir-fried with nam liab (pickled olive) and water morning glory cooked with high heat.

The bulk of reviews agree: consistently good flavor, quality ingredients, the same taste no matter how many times you return. The honest note is that prices are noticeably higher than a typical khao tom kuay shop — expect roughly 250–500 THB per person if you order several dishes — and there are some reviews about slow service, which comes with the territory of an old-school restaurant. You accept that tradeoff for the flavor.

Location is easy — inside Silom Plaza right on Silom Road, walkable from BTS Sala Daeng or MRT Silom. Open from mid-afternoon to late night, typically around 14:00–01:00, with Friday and Saturday running even later. A Silom late-night institution that has been here long enough to become a reference point for khao tom kuay in Bangkok.
mustOrder: Minced pork soup with salted plum
blocks.bestFor: Late dinner or after-midnight meal — group sharing Chinese congee dishes
blocks.libCredit: Illustration: congee · Alpha from Melbourne, Australia / Wikimedia (CC BY-SA 2.0)

blocks.name: Ros'niyom, Silom Complex branch
blocks.signature: Thai single-plate dishes and desserts — stewed pork leg rice, noodles, Yen Ta Fo, mango sticky rice, bingsu
blocks.descHtml:
If you're walking around Silom at lunchtime and want food without standing in the heat to find a place, Ros'niyom at Silom Complex is the most reliable answer. It's a single-plate Thai street food-style restaurant from the iberry group, located on Level B1 in front of Tops. Walk from BTS Sala Daeng exit 4 and you're there in under a minute. Good for office workers who want a familiar Thai plate in a cool, relaxed room without a queue battle — solo, with a work team, or with family, the menu covers enough ground to suit everyone, from noodles to rice plates to desserts.

The dishes reviews mention most and praise consistently are the Yen Ta Fo Pon Fai — a tom yum-inflected noodle soup where many reviewers say they don't need to add a single seasoning, the broth full and well-rounded — and the stewed pork leg rice with tender meat, the char siu-crispy pork plate, and the tom yum pork noodle soup with generous toppings. More adventurous options include moo deng (bouncy pork) with seafood dipping, and Thai basil fried rice. For desserts, mango sticky rice and bingsu both work well in Bangkok's heat. Prices sit mostly at 100–130 THB per dish; a full meal runs around 150–250 THB per person — reasonable for a mall in the middle of Silom.

International visitors specifically mention the photo menu with English descriptions makes ordering easy. Service is quick with plenty of staff. Both cash and QR payment are accepted. Most reviews say "worth it for what you get at this price and location" — a place that does well against what you'd expect. Some reviews note certain dishes are less bold than hoped, or run a touch sweet, but the shop has remained in Silom Complex while surrounding restaurants have changed hands repeatedly — a sign the regulars keep coming back.

Good to know: weekday lunch (roughly 11:30–13:00) gets very crowded with Silom office workers. Come before or after that window for an easier table. Open daily 10:30–22:00, making it a practical choice for lunch, dinner, or an early evening meal after walking around Silom.
blocks.bestFor: Easy lunch or dinner in a Silom mall — solo, family or after-work with friends
blocks.spice: Adjustable — both mild and spicy dishes available

blocks.title: Want to taste more in one trip? Try a food tour or cooking class
blocks.text: If you have limited time but want to cover more ground, a food tour with a guide helps a lot — they'll navigate you through the best spots in Bang Rak-Charoen Krung, order the signature dishes without the guessing, and tell you the story behind each one along the way. If you'd rather be hands-on, Thai cooking classes run from fresh-market visits through to cooking and eating your own meal. Book ahead via Klook or GetYourGuide, pick a time that fits your itinerary, and tackle more places from this list on the other days.

blocks.title: Know before you eat in Silom-Sathorn, Bangkok

items.title: Almost everything is walkable from BTS Sala Daeng / MRT Silom
items.text: Most places on this list are clustered around Silom Road, Convent, Surawong, and Sala Daeng. Get off at BTS Sala Daeng or MRT Silom and walk from there. For the slightly further spots like Charoen Krung, a short Grab ride is easy and cheap.

items.title: Bring cash for street food shops
items.text: Fine dining restaurants and mall-based places accept cards and QR payment. But older street-food shops like Guay Jub Silom and Somtum Convent mostly take cash. Keep small bills on hand — it moves things along.

items.title: Avoid the weekday lunch rush
items.text: Silom-Sathorn is a dense office district. From noon to 13:30 on weekdays, queues form at almost every restaurant. Go before noon or after 14:00 for a comfortable table. Popular dinner spots — especially fine dining — fill up fast, so book or arrive early.

items.title: You can always ask for your spice level
items.text: The Isan and som tam places here are genuinely hot. If you don't eat spicy, tell the staff — say 'phet noi' (a little spicy) or 'no spicy' and they'll adjust. Ordering sticky rice and a cold drink alongside helps too.

items.title: English menus at the bigger places
items.text: Eat Me, Le Du, The Indian Hut, Somtum Der, and the mall restaurants all have English menus and staff who speak English. At older street-side shops there may only be a Thai menu — pointing at a photo or showing a review on your phone always works.

items.title: Tipping isn't mandatory, but it's welcome at sit-down places
items.text: Street food shops don't expect a tip. Sit-down restaurants often include a 10% service charge on the bill already. If it's not included and the service was good, rounding up or leaving spare coins is fine — no fixed rule.

blocks.title: How to plan a full day of eating in Silom-Sathorn
blocks.html:
This neighbourhood feeds you well all day if you sequence it right. For lunch, go for something quick — Guay Jub Silom in Soi Convent, Prachak duck rice in Bang Rak, or Baan Phadthai for pad Thai — these places serve fast and won't slow you down for walking afterwards. If you want to sit in air-con, The Indian Hut or Somtum Der near Sala Daeng are both a short walk from the BTS.

Save dinner for the upgrade. For a special occasion, book Le Du or Eat Me well in advance — they fill up fast, especially on Fridays and Saturdays. For those eating late or finishing a night out, Khao Tom Niyom at Silom Plaza is open until around 3am: order the clams with chili paste and a hot bowl of congee to close the night. Two or three places per day is the right pace — portions at these restaurants are real, so don't rush to fit in too many at once.

blocks.text: Eaten your way through the neighbourhood? A well-placed hotel in Silom-Sathorn means you can walk back after dinner rather than chasing a cab. Boutique lanes to five-star Sathorn — we've sorted the options.

faq.q: Which is the most famous restaurant in Silom-Sathorn?
faq.a: By reputation, Le Du is the standout — Chef Ton's restaurant reached number one on Asia's 50 Best Restaurants in 2023 and has held a Michelin star for years. For the classic street-food institution that all of Bangkok knows, Prachak Roasted Duck in Bang Rak has been selling the same recipe for over a hundred years. Eat Me has been an international dining landmark in Silom since 1998.

faq.q: What are the signature dishes of Silom-Sathorn, Bangkok?
faq.a: The neighbourhood covers a wide range. The most talked-about dishes are the crispy-skin roasted duck and duck rice at Prachak, the crab-and-fermented-fish som tam and fried chicken at Somtum Der and Somtum Convent, Baan Phadthai's 18-ingredient pad Thai sauce, butter chicken and tandoor naan at The Indian Hut, thick-broth guay jub at Guay Jub Silom Soi Convent, and Teochew-style Chinese congee with side dishes at Khao Tom Niyom.

faq.q: Roughly how much do these restaurants cost per person?
faq.a: The range is wide. Street food and single-plate places like Guay Jub Silom, Prachak Roasted Duck, and Ros'niyom run about 60–280 THB per dish. Sit-down restaurants like Somtum Der, The Indian Hut, and Khao Tom Niyom average roughly 250–500 THB per person. Fine dining at Eat Me runs around 1,200–2,500 THB per person, and Le Du is a tasting menu starting around 3,900 THB.

faq.q: Do I need to book in advance for Silom-Sathorn restaurants?
faq.a: Fine dining spots should always be booked ahead — Le Du and Eat Me fill up on most evenings, especially Fridays and Saturdays. Book online or by phone. Street-food and single-plate spots like Prachak, Guay Jub Silom, Somtum Convent, and Khao Tom Niyom are walk-in only, but expect a queue at peak weekday lunch hours when office workers are out in force.

faq.q: Which places are open in the evening or late at night?
faq.a: For late nights, Khao Tom Niyom at Silom Plaza is open until around 1am (and later on weekends), making it the go-to for a post-party meal. Eat Me runs until 1am daily. Most other restaurants close between 21:00 and 23:00. Some street-food shops and older spots may close on weekends or certain days — check the restaurant's page before heading out.
